Cohoes.wildlife_intro:
Cohoes is a mill city squeezed between two rivers, and its wildlife calls match that geography. Norway rats work the old mill blocks, basements, and sewer-age housing near the Mohawk, raccoons den in the chimneys of the brick worker housing, and squirrels cross from the riverside tree canopy straight onto roofs on Van Schaick and Simmons islands. The falls end of town adds rocky, brushy shoreline where skunks and opossums forage at night.

Winter on the Mohawk pushes rodents into the heated mill-era buildings first, because shared walls and old foundation stone leave gaps a rat can widen. Spring brings raccoon mothers into flues above the island neighborhoods, and summer evenings show big brown bats working the river for insects before returning to eaves downtown. Our crew inspects Cohoes homes from foundation stone to ridge cap, removes the animals, and seals the shared-wall and roofline junctions that mill housing hides — in a row of attached homes, sealing only one unit rarely ends the problem.

faqs.q: I hear scratching in my Watervliet attic every winter. What is it?
faqs.a: On Watervliet's tree-lined older streets it is most often gray squirrels that moved in during the fall and stayed for the winter, entering where branches overhang the roof or at a rotted soffit corner. A DEC-licensed Nuisance Wildlife Control Operator can confirm the species from droppings and entry size, remove the animals, and seal the corner — waiting until spring usually means a litter in the same attic.

Watervliet.wildlife_intro:
Watervliet packs a lot of old housing onto a narrow strip of Hudson riverfront, and the calls follow the density. Squirrels work the mature street trees into the attics of the city's doubles and single-family homes, Norway rats hold the oldest blocks and commercial cellars near the river, and raccoons use uncapped chimneys all over the hill streets. It is small-city work: short blocks, shared driveways, and roofs close enough together that animals treat whole streets as one territory.

The river sets the seasons here. Cold Hudson winters drive rats and squirrels into the pre-war housing stock early, spring litters appear in chimneys above the arsenal end of town, and summer brings skunk families out from under porches on the side streets. Our crew starts every Watervliet job with a full exterior pass — porches, additions, and garage roofs included — then removes the animals and seals each opening, because on these tight lots the entry is as often on an addition roof as on the main roof.

faqs.a: Yes — streets backing onto Albany Pine Bush preserve land sit on a nightly route for raccoons, skunks, and opossums moving between barrens cover and neighborhood food sources. The fix is structural: capped chimneys, screened deck and shed voids, and sealed soffits. Our crew checks ground-level denning spots as well as the roof on every Pine Bush-edge inspection.

Colonie.wildlife_intro:
Colonie is Albany County's big suburban town, and its wildlife pressure comes from the seam between subdivisions and the Albany Pine Bush. Gray squirrels and raccoons are constant in the postwar neighborhoods of Latham and Loudonville, groundhogs burrow the larger back lots, and the Pine Bush edge keeps skunks, opossums, and the occasional bat colony circulating through streets that back onto preserve land. Wolf Road's commercial corridor adds Norway rats around dumpsters and older retail buildings.

Colonie's calls peak twice. In fall, squirrels test every soffit in the ranch and split-level subdivisions before the first hard freeze; in spring, raccoon mothers pick chimneys in the older Loudonville streets and groundhogs reopen burrows under sheds. Our crew inspects Colonie homes roof to foundation, removes the animals, and seals entries with the lot's habitat in mind — a house backing onto Pine Bush barrens needs its ground-level voids screened as carefully as its roofline.

faqs.q: Are groundhogs a serious problem in Guilderland?
faqs.a: They are one of the town's steadiest calls, especially west of the suburbs where lots meet fields and horse pasture. Our crew removes the animals and screens the structure's skirt so the next groundhog cannot simply move into the old burrow system.

Guilderland.wildlife_intro:
Guilderland stretches from Albany's western suburbs out to the village of Altamont under the Helderberg escarpment, and the work changes along that gradient. In the suburban east, raccoons and squirrels fill the attics of the Western Avenue corridors; farther west, farm-edge lots draw groundhogs under barns and sheds, skunks around outbuildings, and bats into the eaves of older farmhouses. The Pine Bush covers the town's northeast corner with the same sandy barrens habitat as next-door Colonie.

Spring in Guilderland starts with groundhogs digging out along field edges and raccoon mothers denning in farmhouse chimneys, while the suburbs see the usual fall rush of squirrels ahead of winter. Second properties and barn conversions near Altamont can host a bat colony for a full season before anyone notices. Our crew inspects the house and the outbuildings together on Guilderland calls, removes the animals, and seals the main structure first — a sealed house beside an open barn is only half a solution.
